# Artificial Intelligence Assisted Creativity: Conceptualization, Instrument Development 

# and Validation

Pui Yi Mok[1](#artificial-intelligence-assisted-creativity-conceptualization-instrument-development)[ ](https://orcid.org/0009-0004-4516-4794)\| Hsueh- Hua Chuang[1](mailto:hsuehhua@g-mail.nsysu.edu.tw)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8580-7652)\| Ming- Min Cheng[1,2](#artificial-intelligence-assisted-creativity-conceptualization-instrument-development)[ ](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7085-201X)\| Thomas J. Smith[3](#artificial-intelligence-assisted-creativity-conceptualization-instrument-development)

**Funding:** This work was supported by the National Science and Technology Council, Taiwan; Grant NSTC- 113- 2629- H- 110- 001- SS2. **Keywords:** AI- assisted \| Artificial Intelligence \| creative potential \| creativity \| functional creativity \| ideational creativity \| visual artistic creativity

## ABSTRACT Considering the pivotal role of creativity across various eras and the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in both cre- ative processes and education, this study introduces and provides validity evidence for the AI- assisted Creativity Questionnaire (AICQ). This new 16- item instrument aims to quantify human creative potential in AI- assisted endeavors. Initially, a diverse cohort of 322 university students in Taiwan completed the AICQ from November to December 2023. Through exploratory fac- tor analysis (EFA) of responses from this sample, three distinct factors emerged: (1) AI- assisted functional creativity (AIFC), 

2. AI- assisted visual artistic creativity (AIVAC), and (3) AI- assisted ideational creativity (AIIC). One item was removed due to cross- loading. Subsequently, in September 2024, 330 university students in Taiwan engaged with both the AICQ and the 28- item Creative Behavior Inventory (CBI). Based on responses from this sample, construct validity evidence for the AICQ was examined using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), which affirmed that a three- factor model provided a good fit to the data. Gender differences in AICQ scores were found in these subsequent data. Overall, data from participants provided evidence for the reliability as well as convergent, concurrent, and discriminant validity of the scores obtained from the AICQ.

The involvement of GenAI doesn't replace human creativity but complements it, necessitating human input and decision- making in the process (Epstein et al. [2023)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the).

The integration of AI in creative processes can be classified into four key functions: generators, which aid in brainstorm- ing ideas; blenders, which mix existing concepts for inspiration; transformers, which digitize designs for implementation; and editors, which refine content in the later stages of the creative process (Hwang 2022). These functions span across five appli- cation areas: content creation, information analysis, content en- hancement, information extraction, and data compression. This highlights AI's role as a supportive tool rather than a creator, with broad adoption expected in the future (Anantrasirichai and Bull [2022)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the).

In addition, GenAI is becoming a valuable tool for boosting students' creativity in education. Hutson and Cotroneo (2023) investigated the integration of GenAI in art education. They found that students' conceptualization became more refined with multiple iterations of prompts for the generated artwork by increasing their understanding of what AI can do, and students appreciated how AI enhanced their creativity and ideation pro- cess. Habib et al. (2024), examining how AI affects students' creativity using GenAI (ChatGPT) in an Alternative Uses Test, found that GenAI had the potential to enhance students' cre- ative thinking by assisting students in expanding their ideas during brainstorming sessions.

Despite the increasing interest in how AI impacts human cre- ativity, there is a lack of tools to measure individual creativity in AI contexts. Given the importance of measuring creativity for research and practical applications (Amabile [1983)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the), there has been a demand for the development of assessment tools that keep pace with the technological advancements in cre- ative processes. The current study was inspired by Hoffmann et  al.'s  (2016) Creative Behavior Questionnaire: Digital (CBQD), and its goal of assessing the construct of creative behavior. However, we realized that the CBQD, developed before the rapid development of AI, no longer fully captures the influence of today's technological progress. To bridge this gap, we aimed to design and provide validity evidence for a new instrument tailored to assess creative potential in the AI domain. As suggested by Ivcevic (2009), such an inventory of creative behavior can serve as a preliminary screening tool that can be used prior to conducting laboratory experiments or evaluating an individual's actual creative performance or behavior.

**2 \| Theoretical Framework**

**2.1 \| Creativity**

Creativity, identified as a key 21st- century skill (Trilling and Fadel 2009), involves generating innovative and practical solu- tions within given constraints (Sternberg 1999). According to Runco and Jaeger's  (2012) Standard Definition of Creativity, creativity requires two essential factors: originality and 

effectiveness. While originality is crucial, practical effective- ness is equally necessary for success.

Corazza ([2016)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) expanded this definition by emphasizing “po- tential,” defining creativity as potential originality and effec- tiveness and describing it as a context- embedded and dynamic phenomenon. This suggests that creative inconclusiveness is a crucial phase in the creative process that individuals must nav- igate and show they can manage effectively. While the creative process does not always culminate in a singular clear solution but instead embraces inconclusive outcomes, individuals with high creativity utilize the frustration they encounter due to in- conclusive results constructively, whereas those less creative may drop out.

Creativity consists of both creative potential and creative be- havior, and these must be clearly distinguished in research (Runco 2007; Ivcevic 2009). This study focuses on creative po- tential, which refers to cognitive traits and abilities that con- tribute to creativity, such as personality, divergent thinking, and self- assessed creativity (Ivcevic 2009). On the other hand, creative behavior is the actual performance or product that oc- curs as the concrete result of creative potential (Ivcevic 2009). Runco's (2007) hierarchical framework differentiates these two concepts by revising the “4P” model of creativity (Rhodes 1961) and integrating Simonton's  (2012) additional “P”—persua- sion. The framework asserts that creative potential consists of components that exist without observable creative results (i.e., “person,” “process,” and “press”) as well as components that di- rectly lead to actual creative outcomes (i.e., “product” and “per- suasion”). Additionally, Runco emphasizes the interactions that can occur between these components.

Corazza et al. ([2022)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) suggested that creative potential can be interpreted in up to 15 different ways based on three creativity- relevant frameworks. One of these frameworks—particu- larly relevant to the current study—is the “Four C Model of Creativity” (Kaufman and Beghetto  2009), particularly rele- vant to this study, includes “mini- c” (potential for personal exploration), “little- c” (potential for non- professional creative performance), “Pro- C” (potential for professional- level creativ- ity), and “Big- C” (potential for extraordinary contributions). Additionally, “embedded individual potential” refers to the cre- ative potential shaped by an individual's cultural environment.

**2.2 \| Creativity in Different Contexts and Time Periods**

True to its name, the definition and framework of creativity con- tinually evolves, shaped by various cultures (Boden [1998)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) and historical periods (Sawyer 2011). Sternberg and Karami (2021), for example, recently expanded the theoretical framework of creativity, evolving it from the 6P model to an 8P model. This updated framework retains the six original components of pur- pose, press, person, problem, process, and product, while em- phasizing the increasing significance of propulsion and public recognition in today's context. Unlike intelligence and wisdom, which are primarily analytical, creativity needs a driving force to push boundaries and encourage novelty. Additionally, as 

creativity advances, public acknowledgment becomes essential for evaluation.

The rapid evolution of technology has led researchers to ex- plore creativity enabled by technological advancements across history. Boden's  ([1998)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) framework categorizes computational creativity into three components: combinational creativ- ity (combining unrelated ideas), exploratory creativity (gen- erating new concepts within established frameworks), and transformational creativity (redefining existing conceptual dimensions). Wiggins  (2006) subsequently defined compu- tational creativity as the exploration and support, including simulations, of behaviors exhibited by natural and artificial systems through computational techniques that would be considered creative if performed by humans. Further, at the beginning of 21st century, creativity was transformed into a new form known as digital creativity (Lee 2012), encompass- ing all forms of creative activity facilitated by digital tools (Lee and Chen 2015).

Recent technological advancements have refined the conceptu- alization of creativity, indicating a new phase in its evolution within the AI era. Because GenAI continues to gain widespread adoption and has revolutionized digital processes in many per- sonal and professional activities with the assistance of sophisti- cated deep- learning models such as the Generative Pretrained Transformer, the approach of human- centered AI and hybrid intelligence has been introduced for developing, refining, and executing ideas in diverse creative disciplines (Rafner, Beaty et al. 2023).

In addition, Runco (2023) updated the Standard Definition of Creativity by adding two components—authenticity and inten- tionality—to the original components. The objective behind this update was to distinguish human creativity from artificial cre- ativity. Authenticity emphasizes genuine expression reflecting an individual's true desires, while intentionality underscores humans' innate ability to creatively address problems, contrast- ing with AI's reliance on programmed recognition. Similarly, Wingström et al. (2022) revised the concept of creativity by in- tegrating perspectives from computer scientists and new media artists, outlining 10 distinct definitions of creativity in the era of AI. Two noteworthy updates—interacting with peers or the en- vironment and challenging conventional reality norms—distin- guished creativity with AI assistance from conventional forms of creativity, reflecting AI's transformative impact on creativ- ity. Based on these findings, the current study focuses on a new phase of creativity, marking a notable advancement within the era of AI, known as AI- assisted creativity.

**2.3 \| AI- Assisted Creativity**

AI- assisted creativity occurs when AI serves as either a partner collaborating with individuals to generate creative works, or as an assistant helping individuals in enhance their creativity in various says (Bron [2023)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the). This aligns with the concept of “Co- Cre- AI- tion” proposed by Vinchon et al. (2023) which empha- sizes genuine cooperation, whereby both humans and GenAI contribute to integrated outcomes surpassing individual capa- bilities, thereby fostering augmented creativity.

Research findings indicate that AI can serve as a collaborator or assistant in the creative process, supporting the concept of AI- assisted creativity. For instance, GenAI has assisted composers in music creation by freeing them from certain tasks and deci- sions, enabling them to focus on more creative aspects, while re- taining ultimate decision- making authority (Micchi et al. 2021). It also enhances assisted visualization by functioning as a dual- purpose visual and ideational tool, introducing collaborative elements like prompt engineering, improving visual expression without necessitating artistic skills, and facilitating idea com- munication (Rafner, Zana, et al. 2023). Moreover, the assistance of GenAI in story- writing increases the novelty and usefulness of stories compared to those created on their own, which is par- ticularly apparent when writers requested multiple AI ideas, giving them different starting points and more creative plots (Doshi and Hauser [2024)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the).

In the realm of education, GenAI has the potential to boost cre- ativity by automating processes like brainstorming, idea gen- eration, art and design, music composition, storytelling, and writing. This provides students with diverse starting points for creative projects while also requiring careful management of potential risks (Manditereza and Chamboko- Mpotaringa 2024). This has been demonstrated in empirical research. Rong et al. (2022), for example, conducted an experiment with middle school students, where the group receiving AI and VR fine arts training showed enhanced creativity, concentration, and en- thusiasm compared to the control group undergoing traditional training.

**3 \| Factors Related to AI- Assisted Creativity**

Prior research findings have indicated a positive correlation be- tween students' familiarity with GenAI and their frequency of using it (Chan and Hu[ 2023)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the). GenAI has emerged as a prominent tool for producing high- quality artistic media across diverse domains including visual arts, music, video, and animation (Epstein et al. [2023)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the). Given the fundamental role of these media in the art field, it is reasonable to presume that students in art- related disciplines possess foundational skills or proficiency to effectively utilize AI tools in creating artworks. Therefore, we hypothesize that students in art fields will show greater AI- assisted creativity compared to students in non- art fields.

Gender is considered another potential influential factor, due to its correlation with attitudes toward AI and its effect on self- rated creativity. Research has indicated that males tend to ex- hibit more favorable attitudes toward AI compared to females (Grassini  2023; Sindermann et al. 2021) and to display higher confidence levels and greater engagement with new technolo- gies (Yau and Cheng 2012).

Research on gender differences in creativity has yielded mixed results. Baer and Kaufman ([2008)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) reviewed approximately 74 studies and found no consistent gender differences in creativity. They suggested that environmental factors, such as opportu- nities and societal expectations, may explain the inconsistent findings. Nakano et al. (2021) analyzed 133 studies and reported mixed findings, with some showing women performing bet- ter, others showing men performing better, and the remainder 

3 of 16

varying by factors considered. Hora et al. (2022) conducted a meta- analysis of 259 studies and found a gender gap in self- rated versus other- rated creativity, suggesting women may undervalue their contributions while men overestimate theirs. Additionally, Repeykova et al. (2024) found similar self- rating differences among high- achieving adolescents, with females rating themselves higher in artistic creativity and males rating themselves higher in mechanical/scientific creativity.

Given that this study utilizes a self- rated questionnaire, we propose that males' self- assessed AI- assisted creativity will be higher than that of females.

**4 \| Purpose of this Study**

Considering that measuring creativity is crucial for academic and practical research (Amabile [1983)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the), and there is lack of in- strumentation tailored to evaluate creativity within the realm of AI assistance, this study developed and validated the AI- assisted Creativity Questionnaire (AICQ) to evaluate creative potential in AI- assisted environments, while also exploring group differences in AI- assisted creative potential.

**5 \| Research Hypothesis**

Based on the aforementioned factors related to AI- assisted cre- ativity, the following hypotheses are posited:

**H1.** _Students in art- related majors will show greater AI- assisted creative potential than those in other fields_.

**H2.** _Male students will show greater AI- assisted creative poten-_ _tial than female students_.

**6 \| Questionnaire Development**

The AICQ was developed following three principles. First, McKim's  (2023) guidelines were employed to incorporate ex- isting literature into the scale construction, including liter- ature selection and table creation. Second, we followed the guidelines in Scale Development Theory and Application (DeVellis and Thorpe [2022)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) to define measurement objectives, generate an item pool, and conduct expert reviews and cog- nitive interviews. Finally, the validation process adhered to best practices outlined by Worthington and Whittaker (2006), considering sample size, reporting standards, and utilizing techniques such as factor analysis and structural equation modeling (SEM).

**6.1 \| Item Development**

To develop the items, the first step involved a thorough litera- ture review pertaining to how AI enhances human creativity across fields, focusing on research from the past decade to in- clude recent technological advancements. The justification for each questionnaire item used in this study is detailed in Table 1, providing a comprehensive insight into the influence of AI on 

creativity across different domains based on recent research findings.

In summary, studies have shown that chatbots enhance idea generation and reduce collaboration anxiety, AI tools support writers and improve writing environments, and virtual reality roles stimulate engineering students' creativity. Live feedback from AI boosts team creativity, AI- assisted tools aid in image generation and idea visualization. AI also enhances fan art quality, aids in producing background music, and personalizes event promotions. In gaming, AI enriches in- game creativity, while AI generators elevate web design. Programming courses with robots foster computational thinking and creativity. AI can also revolutionize and stabilize video content through voice cloning and assist in marketing as well as fundraising.

**6.2 \| Content Validity**

Upon drafting the preliminary questionnaire, a focus group— consisting of an instructional technology expert, a creativity specialist, and five Ph.D. students with diverse international backgrounds—was formed to assess evidence for content va- lidity. Subsequently, a cognitive interview was conducted with nine students from a research- oriented university in Taiwan to evaluate their interpretation and understanding of the items, aiming to ensure clarity in the content (DeVellis and Thorpe [2022)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the). Following feedback, amendments were made by removing specific names for software applications to address any reported confusion.

The questionnaire, originally crafted in English, was trans- lated into Chinese and back- translated into English by three Chinese- speaking Ph.D. students to ensure accuracy. An exter- nal interpreter and a Chinese- speaking professor reviewed the bilingual version for final approval.

**7 \| The Present Study**

Two studies were conducted to develop and provide validity evidence for the AICQ. Study 1 employed exploratory factor analysis (EFA) to identify underlying factors, evaluate item characteristics, and explore aspects of creative behavior in the AI domain. Study 2 employed confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to assess the fit of the data to the hypothesized model from Study 1, and provide evidence for convergent, concurrent, and discriminant validity. Both studies also independently tested the research hypotheses (H1 and H2).

Factors were subsequently named based on shared characteristics of observable variables (Watkins 2018).

**8.2.2** \| **Comparing Arts and Non- Arts Students and Gender Differences**

The difference between students was examined using the factors and corresponding questionnaire items that were es- tablished by EFA. For the first research hypothesis (H1), participants were divided into two groups for evaluating: (i) the arts group, including students in art- related fields such as fashion design, product design, music, and theater, and 

1. the non- arts group consists of students in majors such as engineering, humanities, management, mathematics, medi- cine, sciences, social sciences, and technology. For the second research hypothesis (H2), participants were categorized into 

<div></div>

1. male and (ii) female based on self- reported demographics. Welch's _t-_ test (Welch 1938) was used to compare mean AICQ scores between the groups. This method was chosen because it controls Type 1 error rates and is robust compared to Student's _t_- test when homogeneity of variance is not met (Delacre et al. [2017)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the).

**8.3 \| Results**

**8.3.1 \| Data Screening and Management**

No missing values were found among the respondents' re- sponses. Outlying responses, accounting for less than 2% of the dataset and observed within items 8 to 17, were retained for analysis. This decision was based on the belief that these outliers likely represented genuine data points from a distinct subgroup rather than errors in data collection.

the initial data (_N_ = 322), Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests applied to all 17 AICQ items were statistically significant (each _p_ \< 0.001), indicating departure from univariate normality. Mardia's multivariate kurtosis and skewness tests also showed signifi- cance (_p_\< 0.001), suggesting a lack of multivariate normal- ity in the sample. These findings collectively demonstrate a departure from both univariate and multivariate normality assumptions, but statistical significance may have been influ- enced by the relatively large sample size. Descriptive statistics are shown in Table 2. While most items exhibit skewness values below the acceptable threshold of 2.0, item 14 slightly exceeds this threshold at 2.05. However, all kurtosis values fall within 

the acceptable threshold of 7.0, indicating no concerning issues in the dataset. EFA was selected over principal component analysis for identifying a latent factor structure to represent scores from the measurement instrument, as this approach aligns with the study's objective (Fabrigar et al. 1999; Fabrigar and Wegener [2012)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the). Further, given the non- normal distribution and ordinal measurement level of the AICQ items, principal axis factoring was selected as the appropriate EFA extraction method, as it does not necessitate a normal data distribution (Brown [2015)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the).

**8.3.2.2** \| **Factor Analysis.** Preliminary evaluation of the data showed that the sample was well- suited for analysis, with a satisfactory Kaiser- Meyer- Olkin measure (KMO = 0.928). Bartlett's test of sphericity \[_χ_2(136) = 3532.566, _p_ \< 0.001\] also indicated that correlation structure was adequate for fac- tor analyses.

The scree plot (Figure 1) suggested a three- factor solution, with the number of factors aligning with those determined by the Kaiser's  (1960) eigenvalue method. Parallel analysis provided additional evidence for a three- factor solution. Specifically, the eigenvalues of the actual data surpassed those of simulated data up to the third factor. Consequently, based on these results, three factors were interpreted. This 3- factor solution explained 67.37% of the variance (Table 3).

Based on examination of the EFA results, 16 items were re- tained after excluding one item (item 3) from further analy- sis and consideration due to significant cross- loading, with a difference between loadings of less than 0.10 (Güvendir and Özkan 2022). Three factors were identified and named as: (1) AI- assisted functional creativity (AIFC), (2) AI- assisted visual artistic creativity (AIVAC), and (3) AI- assisted ideational cre- ativity (AIIC). The “AIFC” factor comprised 9 items with an associated eigenvalue of 8.30, accounting for 48.80% of the variance. These items cover AI- assisted activities focused on developing tangible products that tackle real- world problems or make meaningful contributions, for example, “generate unique voice tracks or videos” (_α_= 0.78). The “AIVAC” fac- tor comprised 4 items with an associated eigenvalue of 1.97, accounting for 11.59% of the variance. These items cover AI- assisted activities such as “produce a digital art or creative drawing” (_α_ = 0.80). The “AIIC” factor comprised 3 items with an associated eigenvalue of 1.19, accounting for 7.00% of the variance. These items involve AI- assisted activities aim at fos-

The result showed statistically significant differences between arts students (_n_ = 30) and non- arts students (_n_ = 292) for AIFC \[_t_(32.29) = 2.78, _p_ = 0.004\], but not for AIVAC or AIIC. **9 \| Study 2**

**9.1 \| Method**

**9.1.1 \| Participants**

A total of 330 students from various universities in Taiwan par- ticipated in September 2024 (average age = 30.9 years; 64% fe- male, 36% male). The majority (97%) were Taiwanese, with most 

**TABLE 3** \| Eigenvalues and percentage of explained variance for first four factors obtained from exploratory factor analysis.

**Factor** **Eigenvalue**

pursuing Bachelor's (75%) or Master's degrees (24%), and several pursuing Ph.D. degrees (1%).

**9.1.2** \| **Materials**

Participants received the English- Chinese bilingual question- naire, including the AICQ and the 28- item Creative Behavior Inventory (CBI; Dollinger [2003)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the). The CBI, recently re- evaluated with strong reliability evidence (Rodriguez et al. 2023), mea- sures self- reported engagement in creative activities across do- mains like art, music, writing, and problem- solving.

**9.2 \| Data Analysis**

**9.2.1 \| Confirmatory Factor Analysis**

After extracting factors through EFA in Study 1, a CFA was performed using data from the second, independently- collected sample (_N_ = 330) using the R statistical application and lavaan (Rosseel 2012) package to assess construct valid- ity for the AICQ scores. Model fit was evaluated using four indices: root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker- Lewis Index (TLI), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR). As fit crite- ria, an RMSEA value over 0.10 indicates poor fit, 0.08–0.10 suggests mediocre fit, and below 0.08 indicates good fit (MacCallum et al. 1996). For a good fit, CFI and TLI values should exceed 0.95, and SRMR should be less than 0.08 (Hu and Bentler 1999).

**9.2.2** \| **Composite Reliability, Construct Validity, and Concurrent Validity**

To further examine the construct validity evidence for scores obtained from the AICQ, composite reliability was computed, and evidence for both convergent and discriminant valid- ity was evaluated. Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability were used to assess internal consistency of the scale, where the value should be at least 0.70 for scores from the instrument to be considered internally consistent (Cheung et  al.  [2023;](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) Cronbach  [1951)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the). Convergent validity was assessed by exam- ining the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) value (Cheung et  al.  [2023)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the), ensuring it exceeds the 0.5 threshold (Fornell and Larcker  1981). Discriminant validity was examined by comparing the factor correlations with the square root of the AVE value, specifically by assessing whether the correlations 

**Percentage of explained Cumulative percentage variance** **of explained variance**

between factors were smaller than the square root of the AVE for each respective factor (Rönkkö and Cho 2022).

Concurrent validity for the AICQ was assessed by computing the Pearson correlation coefficient between the AICQ scores and the overall scores of CBI. For this concurrent validity as- sessment, it is suggested that the measures to be correlated should be obtained concurrently from the same participants (Kimberlin and Winterstein 2008).

**9.2.3** \| **Comparing Arts and Non- Arts Students and Gender differences**

The differences between students were examined using the fac- tors and corresponding questionnaire items derived from the CFA. The groupings and data analysis methods from Study 1 were applied.

**9.3 \| Results**

**9.3.1 \| Data Screening and Management**

No missing values were found in the data. Outliers, comprising less than 2% of the data, were identified across different CBI and AICQ items. In line with the rationale from Study 1, these outliers were retained for analysis.

**9.3.2** \| **Confirmatory Factor Analysis**

CFA was carried out on the resulting responses to the AICQ, positing a three- factor model based on the results of the EFA in Study 1. Weighted least squares mean and variance adjusted (WLSMV) estimation was used, which is recom- mended for datasets containing variables with either two or three categories (Beauducel and Herzberg [2006)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) or fewer than five categories (Rhemtulla et al. 2012). The decision to utilize WLSMV was strengthened by the sample size surpass- ing 200 participants, rendering it an appropriate choice (Liang and Yang 2014). Consequently, the results from the CFA indi- cated good model fit based on all four fit indices (CFI = 0.978, TLI = 0.974, RMSEA = 0.063, and SRMR = 0.068). Individual items showed good saturation, with all standardized loadings statistically significant and exceeding 0.40. It was concluded that scores from the 16- item instrument adhere to a three- factor structure. The factor structure of the AICQ is depicted in Figure 2.

**9.3.3** \| **Internal Consistency, Composite Reliability, and Convergent and Discriminant Validity**

The values of Cronbach's alpha for the AIFC, AIVAC, and AIIC were 0.95, 0.83 and 0.78 respectively, indicating good internal consistency (Cronbach [1951)](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the). The composite reliabil- ity values for the AIFC, AIVAC, and AIIC factors were 0.95, 0.84, and 0.77 respectively, indicating good reliability (Hair et al. 2009). The AVE values corresponding to AIFC, AIVAC, and AIIC were 0.67, 0.57, and 0.55 respectively, indicating that the convergent validity evidence for the AICQ is adequate. Additionally, the correlations among three factors were lower than the square root of the AVE for each factor, confirming discriminant validity. Tables 5 and 6 provide details pertaining to reliability.

**9.3.4** \| **Concurrent Validity**

All three factors of AICQ were positively correlated with the total scores on the CBI (_r_ = 0.70, _p_ \< 0.001; _r_ = 0.55, _p_ \< 0.001; _r_ = 0.34, _p_\< 0.001, for AIFC, AIVAC and AIIC, respectively), confirming concurrent validity. Further analysis also revealed that all three factors positively correlated with all CBI items. The strongest correlations were AIFC with “Put on a puppet show” (_r_ = 0.66, _p_\< 0.001), AIVAC with “Kept a sketchbook” (_r_ = 0.46, _p_\< 0.001), and AIIC with “Had a piece of literature

**10 \| Discussion and Conclusion**

This study developed a new instrument, the AICQ, comprising 16 items that show evidence of a three- factor structure consist- ing of: AIFC, AIVAC, and AIIC.

Functional creativity refers to the ability to create practical products to address real- life problems or make solid contribu- tions (Cropley and Cropley [2010;](#conflicts-of-interest-corazza-g-e-2016-potential-originality-and-effectiveness-the) e.g. “Generated unique voice tracks or videos”). Visual artistic creativity refers to the ability to create tangible arts such as painting, drawing, and photog- raphy (Heilman and Acosta 2013; e.g. “Produced a digital art or creative drawing”). Ideational creativity emphasizes an in- dividual's ability to generate a wide variety of ideas in terms of fluency, flexibility, and originality (Runco and Mraz 1992; Paulus et  al.  2010; e.g., “Using AI tools like chatbots to ex- plore new ideas or generate fresh insights”). Ideational creativ- ity may occur when generating new insights and surprising findings during group interactions (Paulus et al. 2010; Paulus and Kenworthy  2021; e.g., “Using AI- assisted tools for team
